# Document Set Review — Part 1: Cataloguing the Archive

## Why this step exists

Before anything can be clustered, compared, or synthesized, the raw archive needs to be turned
into something usable: a reliable list of what each of the 31 files actually is, who wrote it,
where it was published, and what it claims. That is the entire purpose of this document. No
interpretation or grouping happens here — that is deferred to Part 2.

The dataset consists of 31 distinct PDF articles. No duplicates were found. Three additional
image files supplied alongside the archive are the assignment brief itself and are not treated
as part of the corpus.

## Extraction method, briefly

Each PDF was first checked for embedded title metadata (`pdfinfo`). Where that metadata was
present and reliable, it was used directly. Where it was missing or generic (7 files had no
embedded title at all; one carried a placeholder PDF/A compliance title instead of the real
one), the first two pages of the actual document were extracted and read to recover title,
authors, venue and abstract by hand. This dual approach is noted explicitly because it explains
why some entries below are more precisely sourced than others.

## The catalogue

Rather than a flat table, the 31 entries are presented here in the order processed, each with a
one-line reference and a short description of its actual contribution — not just its title.

---

### Group of scheduling-optimization papers with a classical OR backbone

- **Gomes, Ravetti & Carrano (2021, Computers & Industrial Engineering)** — a bi-objective
  matheuristic (MILP seeding a variable-neighbourhood search) for no-wait heat-treatment
  scheduling. Reports up to 13% energy savings and 90% tardiness reduction against the
  company's actual practice.
- **Zhang, Song & Wu (2023, IEEE Trans. Cybernetics)** — robust optimization for hot strip mill
  scheduling, solved exactly via an improved Benders' decomposition and heuristically via
  multi-objective PSO for larger instances; treats total job start time as an energy proxy.
- **Wang, Qiao, Zhao & Sutherland (2016, CIRP Annals)** — fuzzy-logic NSGA-II model for batch
  heat-treatment scheduling under uncertain gas heating values, processing times and due dates.
- **Rao & Zhang (2025, J. Physics Conf. Series)** — an improved Grey Wolf Optimizer assigning
  steel billets to furnaces to minimize charging-capacity mismatch and completion time; the
  paper explicitly notes the method needs no additional capital investment.
- **Wang, Liu & Jin (2019, Natural Computing)** — NSGA with a support-vector-regression
  surrogate standing in for expensive simulation, used to evaluate schedule robustness against
  stochastic machine breakdowns in steel rolling.
- **Liu, Wan, Gao, Li & Feng (2019, J. Ambient Intelligence and Humanized Computing)** —
  reformulates hot rolling scheduling as a travelling-salesman problem, solved with NSGA-II and
  a hybrid simulated-annealing/PSO method (SA-MOPSO).
- **Sobottka, Kamhuber & Heinzl (2020, J. Manufacturing and Materials Processing)** — hybrid
  discrete-continuous simulation plus a multi-stage heuristic/metaheuristic for planning
  parallel heat-treatment furnaces; reports roughly 10% overall optimization potential, about
  6 percentage points of which is specifically energy-related.
- **Liu, Yan, Cheng, Yang, Sun & Xue (2020, Journal of Cleaner Production)** — an
  energy-efficient hybrid flow-shop model (EHFSP-FO) that explicitly separates continuous from
  intermittent furnace processing in forging lines.
- **Hidri, Alqahtani, Gazdar & Ben Youssef (2021, Sustainability)** — a generic (non-steel)
  combinatorial scheduling result for identical parallel machines with release dates, delivery
  times, and a no-idle constraint, aimed at minimizing energy-related cost.
- **Xu, Ma & Zhang (2024, Computers & Industrial Engineering)** — three deterministic online
  algorithms, each proved optimal, for reheat-furnace scheduling with a deterioration effect,
  where job information is not known in advance.
- **Benedikt, Alikoç, Šůcha, Čelikovský & Hanzálek (2021, Computers and Operations Research)** —
  proves idle-energy-minimizing scheduling is polynomial-time solvable whenever the idle-energy
  function is concave, and derives the concave energy function and optimal control law for a
  bilinear furnace dynamics model.
- **Han, Tang, Zhang & Cao (2020, IEEE Access)** — a MILP plus an enhanced migrating-birds
  optimization jointly scheduling production and ladle dispatching, to cut ladle-reheating
  energy waste.
- **Wang, Han, Zhao & Wang (2022, Chinese Control and Decision Conference)** — a unified
  constrained multi-objective formulation (CMOP) linking reheating-furnace scheduling to the
  rolling plan, solved with a multi-stage multi-objective evolutionary algorithm (MSMOEA).
- **Zeng, Zheng, Lian et al. (2023, Int. J. Minerals, Metallurgy and Materials)** — a
  data-driven, three-layer dynamic scheduling method (pre-scheduling → adaptive adjustment →
  real-time strategy) for hot metal ladles at the ironmaking–steelmaking interface.
- **Long, Sun, Pardalos, Bai, Zhang & Li (2020, Applied Soft Computing)** — a two-stage approach
  combining offline time-series forecasting of job release times with online chance-constrained
  rescheduling, validated via Monte Carlo simulation.

### Group centred on Digital Twins

- **Müller-Zhang, Kuhn & Antonino (2023, Computers in Industry)** — couples an Asset
  Administration Shell-based digital twin with a Deep-Q-Network agent; proposes two distinct
  RL designs depending on whether jobs arrive in small individualized lots or as a continuous
  high-volume stream.
- **Li, Wang, Yang, Sun, Zhao, Mao & Qie (2024, Expert Systems With Applications)** — an IoT-based
  digital-twin framework that merges hot- and cold-strip rolling data into one shared dataset,
  using an improved LightGBM model to predict rolling force.
- **Li, Jiang, Zhao, Song & Liu (2026, IEEE Trans. Industrial Informatics)** — a "five-dimension"
  digital twin paired with an adaptive large-neighbourhood tabu search (ALTS-DT) for scheduling
  parallel walking-beam reheating furnaces.
- **Javaid & Ullah (2025/2026, Journal of Engineering)** — a human-centric digital twin (framed
  as an Industry 5.0 concept) that ingests operator smartwatch data to manage dynamic
  micro-breaks alongside job-shop scheduling.

### Group applying Reinforcement Learning to energy and scheduling decisions

- **Zeng, Lou, Hu, Fan, Liu & Hu (2024; exact venue not fully recoverable from the extracted
  header)** — uses a large language model, guided by human feedback, to design the reward
  function for a deep-RL job-shop scheduler, with a Kolmogorov–Arnold Network as the policy.
- **Bashyal, Boroukhian, Veerachanchai, Naransukh & Wicaksono (2025, Applied Energy)** —
  multi-agent RL (centralized training, decentralized execution) with an attention mechanism,
  coordinating demand-response and energy management across heavy-industry manufacturing.
- **Wang, Han, Zhao & Wang (2025, IEEE Trans. Industrial Electronics)** — a two-stage
  data-driven DRL framework: offline (ALADIN combined with Soft Actor-Critic) and online (fuzzy
  c-means clustering), for steel-plant energy optimization under supply/demand uncertainty.
- **Shah, Zhou, Wu & Mowbray (2025, Engineering)** — frames electric-arc-furnace scheduling as a
  partially observable Markov decision process, using an attention mechanism plus evolutionary
  policy search, reacting to electricity spot prices and renewable generation.

### Group focused on Explainability and human trust in AI-driven decisions

- **Arunthavanathan, Sajid, Amin, Tian, Khan & Pistikopoulos (2024, AIChE Journal)** — a
  position paper arguing full AI automation is unacceptable in safety-critical layers (SIS,
  shutdown systems), proposing an "Intelligence Augmentation" model with three levels of human
  involvement instead.
- **Wang & Chen (2024, Expert Systems With Applications)** — proposes new explainability
  techniques (decision-tree surrogates, contribution diagrams, improved bar charts) built
  specifically to make genetic-algorithm scheduling outputs understandable to shop-floor
  workers.
- **Morandini et al. (2023, IHIET)** — a literature review of transparency and explainability in
  AI-based planning and scheduling tools, situated within the EU Horizon Europe "TUPLES"
  project.
- **Mehdiyev, Majlatow & Fettke (2024, Cognitive Computation)** — generates multi-objective
  counterfactual explanations (via NSGA-II) for job-shop scheduling, combining predictive
  process monitoring with formal optimization.
- **Theumer, Edenhofner, Zimmermann & Zipfel (2022, CPSL)** — a multi-agent RL approach to
  production control with an added explainability layer, aimed at building operator trust.

### Group on multi-agent and market-based rescheduling

- **Neuer, Marchiori, Ebel, Matskanis, Wolff, Piedimonti & Mathis (2016, IFAC-PapersOnLine)** —
  a multi-agent system using strategic anticipation and virtual-market structures to reallocate
  and reschedule steel products dynamically.

### Prediction-focused paper

- **Duan, Chen, Bao, Xu, Zhang & Yang (2024/2025, Scientific Reports)** — a genetic-algorithm-
  tuned backpropagation neural network predicting heat energy consumption per ton in a steel
  reheating furnace; reports 94.7% accuracy against 90.24% for the standard BP model.

## Data-quality notes worth flagging

- 7 files carried no title in their PDF metadata at all (`Assessing_the_Transparency`,
  `Counterfactual_Explanations`, `Dynamic_reallocation_and_rescheduling`,
  `Explainable_Deep_Reinforcement_Learning`, `GA_BP_prediction_model`,
  `Intelligent_optimization_method`, `Simulation-Based_Multi-Criteria`); all were resolved via
  first-page text.
- 1 file (`A_robust_dynamic_scheduling...`) had a generic PDF/A-compliance title rather than a
  real one; likewise resolved via first-page text.
- The exact publication venue for the LLM-assisted DRL paper (#11 in the ordering above) could
  not be confirmed with full certainty from the extracted header alone — flagged for anyone who
  needs to cite it precisely.
- No duplicate papers were found across the 31 files.

This inconsistency in the raw metadata is itself informative: it is a direct, concrete
illustration of the "fragmented knowledge" the brief describes, and it is why a normalization
pass (this document) had to happen before any topic mapping could begin.

# Document Set Review — Part 2: Mapping the Topic Landscape

## Goal of this step

With 31 papers catalogued individually (Part 1), the next question is structural: which topics
cluster together, which papers act as bridges between clusters, and — most usefully — where is
the knowledge base thick versus thin. This is what determines where Part 3's comparative
analysis should focus its effort.

## Method

Each paper was assigned to one primary topic group based on its stated method and application
(not its keywords alone, since several papers list broad keyword sets that don't reflect their
actual technical contribution). Papers that genuinely combine two techniques in a load-bearing
way (e.g. a paper that is *both* a Digital Twin implementation *and* an RL controller) are
counted in both groups; these dual-membership papers are exactly the bridges the network
analysis cares about.

## Cluster sizes at a glance

| Group | Papers assigned | Share of corpus |
|---|---|---|
| Furnace & mill scheduling (classical OR / metaheuristics) | 15 | 48% |
| Energy systems & sustainability | 6 (+3 shared with the scheduling group) | 19–29% |
| Digital Twins | 5 | 16% |
| Reinforcement Learning for scheduling/control | 6 | 19% |
| Explainable AI (XAI) | 5 | 16% |
| Multi-agent / dynamic rescheduling | 4 | 13% |

(Percentages don't sum to 100% because several papers are counted in more than one group — see
below for exactly which ones and why.)

## What's inside each group

**Furnace & mill scheduling** is the anchor group and by far the largest. Within it, three
recognizable sub-families exist: heat-treatment/soaking-pit batch scheduling (papers on
matheuristics, fuzzy NSGA-II, and simulation-based multi-criteria optimization); reheat-furnace
and hot-rolling scheduling (robust optimization, digital-twin-agent TSP formulations,
release-time forecasting); and furnace idle-energy/logistics control (polynomial-time idle
energy, Grey Wolf billet assignment, ladle dispatching).

**Energy systems & sustainability** overlaps heavily with the first group — three papers
(idle-energy furnace control, online reheat scheduling, and the forging hybrid flow shop) are
just as much "energy" papers as they are "scheduling" papers, which is why they are counted in
both places rather than forced into one bucket.

**Digital Twins** is a small but coherent group: every paper in it explicitly builds a live,
synchronized digital representation of a physical asset (furnace, rolling line, or operator)
and uses it to drive decisions in real time, distinguishing it from papers that merely simulate
offline.

**Reinforcement Learning** papers share a common structure — a Markov Decision Process (or
POMDP) formulation plus a learned policy — but apply it to different problems: job-shop
scheduling, demand response, plant-wide energy optimization, and electricity-market bidding.

**Explainable AI** papers are the most self-contained group: they generally take an existing
optimization method (a GA, an RL agent, a scheduling model) as *given* and ask how its output
can be made interpretable to a human, rather than proposing a new optimization method
themselves.

**Multi-agent / dynamic rescheduling** is the smallest and most loosely defined group; it
overlaps with both RL (multi-agent RL papers) and Digital Twins (a hot-metal-ladle paper whose
adaptive layer is agent-like).

## The bridges — where the groups actually touch

Listing every pairwise connection would be noise; only the papers that materially connect two
otherwise-separate groups matter:

- The Digital-Twin + Deep-Q-Network paper on service-based production connects the Digital
  Twins group directly to the Reinforcement Learning group — it is arguably the single most
  "central" paper in the whole set.
- The digital-twin agent for hot rolling and the digital-twin reheating-furnace paper both
  connect Digital Twins back to the core Furnace & Mill Scheduling group.
- The two-stage DRL energy paper and the DRL electricity-spot-market paper connect
  Reinforcement Learning to the Energy Systems group.
- The multi-agent demand-response paper and the explainable-MARL production-control paper both
  sit at a three-way intersection: Reinforcement Learning, Energy/Multi-agent, and (for the
  explainable one) XAI.
- The production-scheduling-plus-ladle-dispatching paper is the clearest bridge between
  classical furnace/mill scheduling and energy-systems optimization.

## Reading the structure: what's dense, what's thin

The honest picture is a **two-speed archive**. On one side sits a mature, internally consistent
body of classical operations-research work — matheuristics, NSGA-II variants, Benders'
decomposition, PSO — applied to furnace and mill scheduling for at least a decade across
multiple journals. This is not a frontier research area for this organization; it is an
established competency (15 of 31 papers, and the oldest paper in the whole set — from 2016 —
belongs here).

On the other side sits a much thinner, more recent, and more scattered layer of "frontier" AI
work: Digital Twins, Reinforcement Learning, and Explainable AI. These three areas only connect
back to the mature OR core through a small number of bridge papers (six, by count above), and
several papers in this frontier layer have **no peer in the archive at all** — they introduce a
technique nobody else in the set pursues:

- The process-safety position paper (AI vs. Intelligence Augmentation) is conceptually adjacent
  to the XAI group but technically isolated — it is the only paper discussing safety-layer
  automation (SIS, emergency shutdown) rather than scheduling or energy optimization directly.
- The multi-agent virtual-market rescheduling paper and the human-centric Industry-5.0 digital
  twin paper are each the only example of their specific technique in the set.
- The generic green-scheduling-of-parallel-machines paper is the one entry with no
  steel-industry framing whatsoever — pure combinatorial theory, only loosely on-topic via its
  energy objective.
- The LLM-assisted DRL paper is the newest and most methodologically distinct entry (it is the
  only paper combining a large language model with reinforcement learning) — a genuine frontier
  with nothing else in the archive building on it yet.

## Why this matters going forward

This asymmetry — a deep, validated OR foundation next to a thin, scattered set of AI
capabilities — is not just a descriptive fact. It is the single most useful thing this mapping
exercise produces, because it tells Part 3 exactly where the productive tension lies: not
between "old" and "new" for their own sake, but between a body of work that can *prove* its
answers are good and a body of work that can *react* faster than proof allows. That tension —
provable quality vs. real-time responsiveness — is the fault line worth exploring next.

# Document Set Review — Part 3: Where the Approaches Actually Disagree

## Purpose

Part 2 identified a structural gap between a mature classical-OR core and a thinner, scattered
layer of AI-driven approaches. This section does not try to resolve that gap yet — it deliberately
sharpens it, by picking the three points of genuine disagreement in the literature and laying
out both sides plainly. The goal is tension, not premature compromise; Part 4 is where the
reconciliation happens.

---

## Tension A — Provable optimization vs. learned, reactive optimization

The classical camp here — the matheuristic MILP+MOVNS heat-treatment scheduler, the
Benders-decomposition hot-strip-mill model, the fuzzy NSGA-II batch scheduler, the Grey Wolf
billet-charging optimizer, the surrogate-assisted NSGA for stochastic breakdowns, the
digital-twin-agent TSP/NSGA-II/SA-MOPSO hot-rolling model, and the CMOP/MSMOEA furnace-plus-
rolling co-optimizer — shares one defining trait: it can, in at least part of its formulation,
*prove* something about the quality of its answer. The matheuristic paper is explicit about
this: part of its method uses an exact MILP solve specifically to guarantee an
energy-cost-optimal Pareto extreme, with the metaheuristic search only responsible for
improving the tardiness side. That is a real, auditable guarantee, not a marketing claim.

The reinforcement-learning camp — the Digital-Twin-plus-DQN production planner, the
LLM-assisted job-shop scheduler, the multi-agent demand-response system, the two-stage DRL
energy framework, and the POMDP-based electricity-market scheduler — offers no such guarantee.
A trained policy is empirically good on the distributions it was trained and tested on; nothing
in these papers certifies worst-case behaviour the way the matheuristic's MILP step does. What
RL buys instead is speed at the moment of decision. The DQN paper is the cleanest illustration
of the actual cost-benefit here: training its policy from scratch for a four-job scenario took
roughly ten hours, and re-training after a change took anywhere from fourteen minutes to
several hours depending on problem size — but once trained, the policy makes a scheduling
decision essentially instantly, which is precisely what let the same paper design a
continuous-arrival variant meant for live, ongoing deployment. Compare that to the
matheuristic paper's own reported runtime: up to 2.5 hours for a single re-optimization on
roughly 100 jobs. If conditions change faster than 2.5 hours allow, the matheuristic simply
cannot keep up — but it will always be able to tell you, after the fact, how close to optimal
its answer was. The RL policy can keep up, but nobody in these papers can tell you how far from
optimal its answer might be in an unseen situation.

Neither side is wrong; they are answering different questions. The matheuristic family answers
"what is the best schedule, and how do we know?" The RL family answers "what is a good enough
schedule, right now, given everything just changed?"

## Tension B — Live digital representation vs. deployable static modelling

Digital Twin papers — the DQN-coupled production planner, the IoT-based cold/hot-strip data
unifier, the digital-twin-agent hot-rolling model, and the five-dimension reheating-furnace
twin with adaptive tabu search — all share an infrastructure requirement that the rest of the
archive does not: they need a continuously synchronized, standardized representation of the
physical plant (Asset Administration Shells in one case, an IoT "data continent" in another)
before any scheduling decision can even be made. This buys real responsiveness to disruption:
the reheating-furnace twin paper tracks charging and discharging times and slab positions
live, and the IoT framework's whole premise is that hot-strip and cold-strip rolling data used
to sit in separate "information silos" that prevented any collaborative optimization at all —
the digital twin is presented as the fix for exactly that problem.

The classical scheduling and simulation papers — the by-product-gas rolling-horizon MILP, the
polynomial-time idle-energy furnace model, and the discrete-continuous simulation of parallel
heat-treatment furnaces — need none of that infrastructure. They work from a mathematical model
of the process (a bilinear furnace model, a gas-flow balance equation) and a periodic data
snapshot, not a live synchronized twin. This is why they are deployable today on real production
data — the matheuristic and by-product-gas papers both validate against actual plant datasets,
not virtual pilots.

That last point cuts the other way for the Digital Twin side, and it is worth saying plainly:
every Digital Twin paper in this archive is demonstrated on a virtual or pilot-scale system —
the DQN paper's own case study is explicitly a *virtual* aluminum cold-rolling mill built by an
equipment vendor, not a live production line. The technology that best matches the real-time,
reactive requirement is also the one with the least evidence, in this archive, of production
readiness.

## Tension C — Explainability as trust infrastructure vs. explainability as overhead

The XAI-oriented papers — the process-safety position paper on AI vs. Intelligence
Augmentation, the decision-tree/contribution-diagram techniques for genetic algorithms, the
TUPLES literature review on transparent planning tools, the NSGA-II-based counterfactual
explanation generator for job-shop scheduling, and the explainability layer added to a
multi-agent RL production controller — are motivated by something none of the performance-
focused papers mention at all: accountability when a human has to act on, or override, a
machine's decision. The process-safety paper states this as close to an absolute rule —
compliance with IEC/ISA-84 functional-safety standards requires a manual shutdown process
alongside any automated safety-instrumented system, meaning full automation without a human
override is not just undesirable but non-compliant in that specific layer. The GA-explainability
paper frames its own motivation almost identically, just from the shop floor rather than the
safety office: without explainability, workers may simply not accept the algorithm's output,
regardless of how good it is.

Set against that is a group of papers that report strong quantitative results with no
explainability apparatus whatsoever: the Benders-plus-PSO hot-strip-mill scheduler, the
LLM-assisted DRL job-shop scheduler, the two-stage energy-optimization DRL framework, and the
electricity-spot-market POMDP scheduler. None of these treat interpretability as a design
requirement, and nothing in their evaluation suggests it cost them anything in performance.

The honest tension is that explainability is not free when it is added — the counterfactual-
explanation paper needs to run a *second* multi-objective optimization (again via NSGA-II) just
to generate explanations for the output of the first one. Demanding explainability everywhere
would tax every one of the performance-focused papers above for a benefit they may not need,
since none of them sit in a human-override-required context. Demanding it nowhere risks
exactly the failure mode the process-safety paper warns about: correct but incomprehensible
decisions in a context where a human is legally required to be able to intervene.

---

## What these three tensions have in common

Read side by side, all three disagreements are really one disagreement wearing different
clothes: certifiable, auditable, slower decision-making versus fast, adaptive, less-verifiable
decision-making. That is true whether the comparison is optimization method (Tension A),
data infrastructure (Tension B), or decision transparency (Tension C). Part 4 does not attempt
to declare a winner between these — it proposes a structure that puts each capability where its
strength matters and its weakness is contained.

# Document Set Review — Part 4: Putting the Pieces Back Together

## Starting point

Part 3 left three open tensions, all variations of the same trade-off: certifiable, auditable
decisions versus fast, adaptive ones. This section does not pick a side. Instead, it proposes an
arrangement where each capability sits exactly where its strength is decisive and its weakness
is contained by something else in the same system — following the same logic the process-safety
paper already applies at the level of individual safety layers, generalized here to the whole
scheduling problem.

## Walking through how a decision would actually get made

The clearest way to describe this proposal is to follow a single scheduling decision from start
to finish, rather than list abstract layers.

**Before anything else happens**, the decision space is already bounded by physics and by rule,
not by any AI component. No-wait flow constraints, sequence-dependent setup times, furnace
temperature and cooling-rate limits, gas-holder safety bounds, and — critically — the
safety-instrumented-system rule that a shutdown always keeps a manual override path, are all
fixed inputs that no optimization or learning component is allowed to override. This is the
non-negotiable floor everything else operates inside.

**The system then needs to know what is actually happening on the floor right now.** This is
where a Digital Twin backbone earns its place: every furnace, ladle, mixing station and job is
represented as a standardized, continuously updated digital asset, the way the
Asset-Administration-Shell-based production planner and the five-dimension reheating-furnace
twin both do it. This step exists specifically to remove the "information silo" problem
documented in the IoT-based cold/hot-strip paper, where two adjacent production stages
literally could not see each other's data. Without this shared live picture, neither of the
next two steps has anything reliable to work from.

**A decision then actually has to be made, and it has to be made twice, at two different
speeds.** For minute-to-minute dispatch — reacting to a machine breakdown, an updated
electricity spot price, or a shift in job-arrival timing — a trained reinforcement-learning
policy responds essentially instantly, the way the continuous-arrival RL design and the
attention-based electricity-market scheduler both do. But that fast policy needs to be kept
honest. On a slower cadence — daily or weekly, matching the roughly 2.5-hour runtime the
matheuristic paper reports for its own re-optimization — a certified matheuristic or
metaheuristic run (in the spirit of the MILP-plus-migrating-birds ladle-and-production
scheduler) re-anchors the plant-wide plan against a provably good baseline. The relationship
between the two is not that one replaces the other; it mirrors how the matheuristic paper
itself uses an exact MILP solution to seed and regularize its own local search — the same
principle, applied here at the level of two different tools instead of two phases of one
algorithm.

**Finally, someone has to be able to trust — and where necessary, override — what just
happened.** This is not applied uniformly, because Part 3 already showed that would be wasteful.
Wherever a human is required to approve or intervene — a safety shutdown, an operator-facing
schedule change, the kind of worker-facing disruption the GA-explainability paper worried about
— the system owes that human an explanation, built the way the decision-tree/contribution-
diagram techniques or the counterfactual-explanation approach ("what would have avoided this
delay?") do it. Wherever the loop is fully automated and the stakes per decision are low — an
overnight energy-price forecast, a back-office spot-market bid — no such explanation layer is
imposed, because nothing in the archive suggests it would buy anything there beyond
computational cost.

## Why this specific arrangement, and not some other one

Three design choices deserve to be defended explicitly, since each one directly answers a
tension raised in Part 3:

*Why keep the matheuristic loop at all, if the RL loop is faster?* Because nothing in the RL
literature in this archive certifies worst-case behaviour, and the matheuristic literature
explicitly can. Removing the certified loop would mean the plant has no periodic check that the
fast, learned policy has not drifted into a bad region — a check the matheuristic naturally
provides as a byproduct of doing an exact solve.

*Why insist on a Digital Twin layer, given every Digital Twin paper in this archive is a
pilot or virtual deployment rather than a live one?* Because the alternative — scheduling off
of periodic, siloed snapshots — is precisely the failure mode the IoT cold/hot-strip paper
describes as blocking collaborative optimization entirely. The infrastructure cost is real and
should be budgeted for honestly (see the rollout note below), but the problem it solves does
not go away by ignoring it.

*Why make explainability selective instead of mandatory everywhere?* Because the archive itself
shows both extremes are wrong. Nowhere is a hard requirement: several strong-performing papers
(the Benders-plus-PSO scheduler, the two-stage DRL energy framework) show no explainability
cost at all. Nowhere is also wrong: the process-safety paper treats human oversight in
safety-critical layers as close to a compliance requirement, not a nice-to-have. Tying the
requirement to decision stakes, rather than applying it as policy everywhere, is the only
reading of the source material that is consistent with both facts at once.

## Before this goes plant-wide

Every Digital Twin implementation found in the archive is a single-line or virtual-scale
demonstration — the DQN-based planner's own case study runs on a vendor-built *virtual* cold
rolling mill, not a live one. The honest recommendation that follows from that fact is to pilot
this arrangement on one line first, the same way the simulation-based multi-criteria paper
piloted its method on a single casting manufacturer, rather than assuming the underlying
Digital Twin infrastructure is already production-ready across a full plant.

# Briefing for Leadership
**Rethinking How We Schedule Furnaces and Rolling Mills**
*Built from a review of 31 sources spanning classical scheduling theory, digital twins,
reinforcement learning, and explainable AI (full detail in Parts 1–4 of this review)*

---

## Attention

Ask a simple question: how much of what we spend on energy in this plant is actually
unavoidable? The literature we reviewed gives an uncomfortable answer for heat treatment
specifically — the heating step alone can account for up to 70% of total process energy
consumption. That is not a rounding error in the budget; it is the budget.

And the losses compound where we would least expect them to be optimized away: one
peer-reviewed study of an actual industrial heat-treatment line found that better scheduling —
not new equipment, just better sequencing and timing decisions — recovered up to 13% in energy
costs and cut tardiness by as much as 90%, compared to what the plant was already doing
manually. A separate furnace-charging study reported comparable operational gains while
explicitly requiring **no additional capital investment** at all. These are not projections.
They are measured results from real production data.

The uncomfortable part is that we are almost certainly leaving equivalent gains on the table
today, simply because our own scheduling decisions are not built around these methods.

## Interest

The good news is that none of this requires speculative technology. Three capabilities, each
already validated in the published literature, are ready to be combined:

First, **reinforcement-learning-based scheduling** can react to conditions changing in real
time — a machine breaking down, an electricity spot price spiking, an unplanned order arriving
— in a fraction of the time a traditional re-optimization run would take. One published system
built specifically for this purpose can make a scheduling decision almost instantly once
trained, compared to the multi-hour runtimes that classical optimization solvers typically
need for a comparable re-plan.

Second, **digital twins** solve a problem we already recognize by name: information silos.
One study found that hot-strip and cold-strip rolling — two stages of the same production
line — historically could not share data in a way that allowed any joint optimization at all.
A digital twin, built as a single live, standardized representation of every asset on the
floor, is the documented fix.

Third — and this is the part worth emphasizing to skeptics — none of this requires abandoning
what we already do well. The literature we reviewed contains a deep, mature body of classical
scheduling and optimization research (matheuristics, genetic algorithms, robust optimization)
specifically applied to furnace and mill operations, spanning more than a decade of validated
publications. The right move is not to replace that expertise with newer AI methods. It is to
let each do what it is actually good at.

## Desire

The obvious objection is trust: are we comfortable letting automated systems make more of these
decisions? The literature itself raises this concern before we do, and takes it seriously. One
paper we reviewed is explicit that removing humans entirely from safety-critical decisions —
emergency shutdowns, safety-instrumented systems — is not just risky but, in many jurisdictions,
non-compliant with functional-safety standards that require a manual override path.

Our proposed approach is built around that concern rather than around it:

- Physical and safety constraints stay completely outside any AI system's authority — they are
  fixed inputs, not optimization targets.
- Fast, reactive scheduling (the reinforcement-learning layer) is checked periodically against
  slower, fully auditable optimization runs, so speed is never purchased at the cost of losing
  a certified baseline entirely.
- Explainability is built in wherever a person has to approve or override a decision — using
  techniques the literature already demonstrates, like plain-language "what change would have
  avoided this delay" explanations — and deliberately left out of low-stakes, fully automated
  back-office decisions where it would only slow things down for no real benefit.

This is not a black box we are asking leadership to trust blindly. It is a system designed, from
the published evidence, to be transparent exactly where transparency matters and no more than
that.

## Action

We recommend the following, in this order:

1. **Run a single-line pilot.** Every digital-twin implementation we found in the literature was
   itself demonstrated on a single line or a virtual/pilot-scale system — we should follow that
   same cautious path rather than assume plant-wide infrastructure is ready today.
2. **Keep our existing scheduling logic running in parallel** as the certified baseline against
   which the new reactive system is measured, not as something to be immediately retired.
3. **Design the explanation interface first, not last.** Operator buy-in depends on people
   understanding *why* a schedule changed — build that visibility into the pilot from day one.
4. **Set a fixed six-month checkpoint** against the same metrics the literature already
   validates — total energy cost, total tardiness, and machine utilization — so pilot results
   are directly comparable to the published benchmarks cited above, not just internally
   plausible.

The literature review is done. What we need next is a scoped pilot, not another round of
research.
